lesson.title: H.M. and the Case That Redefined How Memory Works in the Brain
lesson.summary: Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new long term declarative memories after the onset of brain damage, most famously documented in the case of patient H.M., whose surgically altered hippocampus left him unable to consciously remember any new experience for long while his memories from before the surgery, and his capacity for learning new physical skills, remained largely intact.
lesson.body:
Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new long term declarative memories following brain damage or injury, even though briefly holding information in mind, general intelligence, and personality can remain completely intact. It is worth being clear about the direction of this deficit: anterograde amnesia affects memory for things that happen after the injury, going forward in time, different from retrograde amnesia, the loss of memories formed before an injury. A person with pure anterograde amnesia can typically still remember their life before the damage occurred, they simply cannot lay down new long term memories from that point onward.

This condition connects directly to the role of the hippocampus, a brain structure essential for consolidating new experiences into stable, lasting declarative memory, meaning memory for facts and events that can be consciously recalled. When the hippocampus and nearby medial temporal lobe structures are damaged, a person can often still hold a conversation normally because short term or working memory does not depend heavily on the hippocampus, but the moment attention shifts away, whatever was just experienced fails to get consolidated into durable long term storage and is effectively lost for good.

The single most influential case in the study of anterograde amnesia is that of a patient long referred to in the research literature only as H.M., to protect his privacy during his lifetime, and identified publicly as Henry Molaison only after his death. In the early 1950s, H.M. underwent surgery, performed by William Scoville, that removed medial temporal lobe structures including the hippocampus on both sides of his brain, intended as a treatment for severe, medication resistant epilepsy. The epilepsy improved, but the surgery left H.M. with profound and permanent anterograde amnesia. He was studied for decades afterward, most extensively by researcher Brenda Milner and later by Suzanne Corkin, and despite meeting the same researchers repeatedly over years, he would greet them as strangers each time, effectively living in an extended present.

One of the most theoretically important findings from H.M.'s case was a striking exception to his amnesia. When taught new motor skills, such as a mirror tracing task requiring him to draw while only seeing his hand in a mirror, H.M. improved steadily across repeated practice sessions, just as a person with a normal memory would, even though he had no conscious recollection of ever having practiced the task before, or of the researchers working with him on it. This dissociation between his profound loss of declarative, consciously accessible memory and his preserved procedural, skill based memory was powerful evidence that memory is not one single unified system, but is supported by at least somewhat separate brain systems for different kinds of learning.

H.M.'s case, alongside later research on other patients with similar damage, fundamentally reshaped how psychologists and neuroscientists understand the hippocampus. Rather than serving as a general storehouse for all memory or intelligence, which H.M.'s largely intact reasoning and personality argued against, the hippocampus appears to play a much more specific role: helping form and consolidate new declarative memories in the period after learning, without being the final permanent storage site for those memories once they are fully consolidated. Few single cases in the history of psychology have shaped an entire field's understanding of a cognitive system as much as this one did.
